newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Sudan's Bashir calls for ceasefire with rebels.
newsitem.headline: Sudan's Bashir calls for ceasefire with rebels.

text.p: Sudanese President Omar Hassan al-Bashir on Tuesday called for a ceasefire in the gruelling 14-year civil war with the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) rebels in the south of the country.

"We believe that the war should come to an end. In this respect we have requested for a ceasefire with the faction of Dr. John Garang," Bashir told a news conference after talks with South African President Nelson Mandela.

Bashir's visit was requested by Mandela and is taking place against the background of an African peace initiative under the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) chaired by Kenyan leader Daniel Arap Moi.
The Sudanese president said his government would talk to Garang's rebels in the framework of the IGAD intiative in a series of meetings set to begin in Nairobi on August 19.

The war in Sudan, Africa's largest country in size, has pitted Christian and animist rebels in the south against the Moslem and Arabised north. The rebels want greater autonomy or independence from the north.
Bashir, who arrived in South Africa on Monday, is the latest in a long list of African leaders to seek peacemaking advice from South Africa's first black president.
Since being freed from an apartheid jail in 1990 Mandela has contributed to peace efforts in Angola, Algeria, Lesotho, Swaziland, Burundi, Nigeria and the former Zaire.

Mandela told reporters at his state home in Pretoria that although the Sudanese government had signed an agreement with six other rebel groups in April, the key dispute with the SPLA had to be solved.
"Until both these two sit down together and reach a settlement there can be no peace in that country," Mandela said.
"I believe both of them genuinely want peace," he added.

But the SPLA has consistently refused to agree to a ceasefire with Khartoum, arguing that it was advancing on at least three fronts and a ceasefire would merely give the government breathing space to play for time and rebuild its forces.

Present at the South African talks was Garang's former SPLA comrade-in-arms Riek Machar, now commander of the armed forces of the rebel groups allied with the government and also newly appointed President of the Co-ordination Council of Southern States set up under the April accord.
Machar said any refusal by Garang to attend the Nairobi talks may be seen as a sign the rebel chief had political ambitions for the whole country.
"Why sacrifice lives? Why destroy material? Unless there is another agenda the Sudanese people do not know," he said.

Bashir said the agreement with the non-SPLA rebels had laid the foundation for a multi-ethnic, multi-religious, secular state. Machar backed the deal, saying the original aims of winning political rights for south Sudan had been achieved.
"Political issues that were the root causes of the war have been addressed," he said.

The agreement included provision for a four-year transition period after which a referendum would be held to determine whether southern Sudan would become part of a united country or of a federal state. Alternatively it could choose to secede to become entirely independent.
Machar declined to comment on the current military situation or the strength of his own forces, which are now ranged against the SPLA, and urged Garang to accept the ceasefire.
"I hope he (Garang) does not opt for a military solution, because he would just be fighting his brothers," Machar said.
Also present at the talks on Tuesday was Malaysian special representative Tan Sri Ahmad Kamil Jaafar, who recently met the SPLA. "Our only motive is to assist in the removal of conflict," he said.
